title: Job 14:13–22
context: Job, still speaking, voices a longing that God would hide him in Sheol until his wrath passes and then remember him. He asks, If a man dies, will he live again?, and imagines God calling and Job answering. Hope and doubt are both present: the wish is followed by renewed complaint that God watches his sin and wears away human hope as water wears stone. The speech raises the question of life after death without settling it; later Christian readers have connected it with Job 19:25-27 and 1 Corinthians 15, but those are later readings.

verses.text: “Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would keep me secret until your wrath is past, that you would appoint me a set time and remember me!
verses.arminianNotes: Job wishes that God would hide him in Sheol until his wrath has passed and then remember him. Arminian readers see a remarkable longing for God’s favor that reaches even beyond death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Sheol, the realm of the dead, is here imagined as a hiding place rather than an end. Job pictures God’s wrath as temporary and his remembrance as the final word.

verses.text: If a man dies, will he live again? I would wait all the days of my warfare, until my release should come.
verses.arminianNotes: If a man dies, will he live again? Arminian readers note that some read this as a hopeful question pointing toward life beyond death, while others read it as a wish Job cannot yet affirm. The text leaves it open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the question open within Job’s speech. Many Christians later read it alongside Job 19:25-27 and 1 Corinthians 15, but those connections are later readings rather than the speech’s own settled answer.

verses.text: You would call, and I would answer you. You would have a desire for the work of your hands.
verses.arminianNotes: Job imagines that God would call and he would answer, and that God would long for the work of his hands. Arminian readers see Job grasping for a restored relationship with the God who made him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the beauty of Job’s picture of God desiring his creature. Even in complaint, Job believes that God’s deepest disposition toward his handiwork may be love.

verses.text: But now you count my steps. Don’t you watch over my sin?
verses.arminianNotes: But now God counts his steps and watches over his sin. Arminian readers see Job’s hope collapsing back into his present experience of being scrutinized and pressed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the sudden turn from longing to complaint. Job’s faith and despair sit side by side in the same speech, as they often do in the lament psalms.

verses.text: My disobedience is sealed up in a bag. You fasten up my iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says his disobedience is sealed in a bag and his iniquity fastened up. Arminian readers report two readings: God storing up his sins for judgment, others as God sealing them away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image is debated and can be read either as accusation or as hidden mercy. Job may mean that God keeps a careful record against him, which fits the surrounding complaint.

verses.text: “But the mountain falling comes to nothing. The rock is removed out of its place.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says that even mountains fall and rocks are moved from their place. Arminian readers see Job finding examples of slow, relentless erosion that mirror his own experience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the images of collapsing mountains and shifting rock stress that nothing on earth is permanent. Job applies this to human hope in the next verse.

verses.text: The waters wear the stones. The torrents of it wash away the dust of the earth. So you destroy the hope of man.
verses.arminianNotes: As water wears away stones and torrents wash away soil, so God destroys the hope of man. Arminian readers hear Job’s bitter accusation, spoken from pain, that God himself erodes human hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the stark charge that God destroys hope. The book does not endorse every word Job speaks in anguish, yet God later says Job spoke rightly in contrast to the friends (42:7).

verses.text: You forever prevail against him, and he departs. You change his face, and send him away.
verses.arminianNotes: God prevails over man forever; he changes his face and sends him away. Arminian readers see Job describing death as God’s overpowering act, from which no one can resist.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the changed face may suggest the effects of death or aging. Job sees God as the one who finally sends every person away from life.

verses.text: His sons come to honor, and he doesn’t know it. They are brought low, but he doesn’t perceive it of them.
verses.arminianNotes: A man’s sons may be honored or brought low, and he does not know it. Arminian readers see Job grieving the separation of death, which cuts the dead off from those they love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job, who has already lost his children, speaks of not knowing their fate. The pain of the verse is sharpened by his own story in chapter 1.

verses.text: But his flesh on him has pain, and his soul within him mourns.”
verses.arminianNotes: Only his own flesh feels pain, and his soul mourns within him. Arminian readers see Job ending his speech with personal anguish rather than resolution, an honest close to a hard lament.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Job’s reply ends in sorrow, not certainty. The book allows his question to stand unanswered for now, to be taken up again later in the dialogue.
